extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York; framers, delegates, and readers considering the proposed U.S. Constitution (late-18th-century public)
extracted.subtask_description: Argument and evaluative criteria for designing an energetic, accountable executive in a republican constitution: defines what makes an executive 'energetic' and what constitutes 'safety' in a republic, and critiques plural executives and executive councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of Executive Energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy in the Executive is essential to protection against foreign attacks, steady administration of the laws, protection of property from irregular combinations, and the security of liberty against ambition, faction, and anarchy. A feeble Executive implies feeble execution of government and thus bad government in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of Republican Safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people, secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety must be maintained alongside executive energy; the executive should remain dependent on the people and personally responsible to them so that abuses can be checked by public opinion and by removal or punishment when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive promotes energy
rubrics_metrics.description: That unity is conducive to energy will not be disputed. Decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity can be destroyed either by vesting power in multiple magistrates of equal authority or by vesting it ostensibly in one man who is subject to the control/co‑operation of others (counsellors). Where unity exists, decisions are more decisive, active, secret when necessary, and prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of magistrates undermines effective execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever two or more persons are engaged in any common enterprise or pursuit, there is always danger of difference of opinion. If it be a public trust or office, in which they are clothed with equal dignity and authority, there is peculiar danger of personal emulation and even animosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural executives tend to produce dissensions that lessen respectability, weaken authority, distract plans and operations, impede or frustrate important measures in critical emergencies (especially war), and may split the community into violent factions. Historical examples cited include Roman Consuls and substituted Tribunes; the Achaeans' experiment with two Praetors is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive councils (advisory bodies with binding or necessary concurrence) weaken the ostensible executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Vesting it ostensibly in one man, subject, in whole or in part, to the control and co‑operation of others, in the capacity of counsellors to him, will tincture the exercise of the executive authority with a spirit of habitual feebleness and dilatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A council constitutionally necessary to operations invites artful cabals, diversity of views that enervate administration, and routine delays; even absent cabal, mere diversity of opinion weakens executive vigor and expedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal responsibility (accountability) is essential; plurality conceals faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility is of two kinds to censure and to punishment. The multiplication of the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection in either case; it often becomes impossible, amidst mutual accusations, to determine on whom the blame or the punishment of a pernicious measure ought really to fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural executives enable shifting/blame‑shifting and collusion, leaving public opinion in suspense about the real author of mismanagement. This diminishes the two greatest securities for faithful exercise of delegated power: the restraints of public opinion and the opportunity to discover misconduct for removal or punishment. Example: the governor of the State coupled with a council produced scandalous appointments and mutual blame, leaving the people unsure who was responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation is fitting for legislature but harmful for executive dissension
rubrics_metrics.description: In the legislature, promptitude of decision is oftener an evil than a benefit. The differences of opinion, and the jarrings of parties in that department, though they may sometimes obstruct salutary plans, yet often promote deliberation and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advantages of plurality that apply to legislative deliberation (promoting caution, checking majority excesses) do not apply to the executive; in the executive, dissension is 'pure and unmixed' disadvantage without counterbalancing good, because it continually embarrasses and weakens execution from start to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single executive is easier to confine and monitor
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power is more easily confined when it is ONE; that it is far more safe there should be a single object for the jealousy and watchfulness of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single magistrate provides a clear focus for public vigilance and censure; being alone he will be more narrowly watched and suspected and cannot unite as great a mass of influence as several persons might when combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small multiperson executives risk dangerous combinations of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers must be so great as to render combination difficult, or they are rather a source of danger than of security. The united credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty, than the credit and influence of either of them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils or small groups (e.g., from six to a dozen) can be combined by an artful leader, producing greater danger than a single ambitious individual; historical example: the Decemvirs of Rome were more to be dreaded in usurpation than any one of them would have been.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of a large executive council is a practical disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the council should be numerous enough to answer the principal end aimed at by the institution, the salaries of the members, who must be drawn from their homes to reside at the seat of government, would form an item in the catalogue of public expenditures too serious to be incurred for an object of equivocal utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond theoretical objections, a large council imposes significant recurring public costs and burden of residence that weigh against its utility.
